adversarial_test_results.prompt: The Harlan County Fair opened on a grey Thursday morning, and the smell of fried dough and wet grass hung over the grounds before the first bus arrived. Vendors had come before dawn to claim the same spots their families had kept for three generations, and by eight the gravel lanes were lined with trailers, folding tables, and hand-painted signs. A man named Dale Whitaker sold honey from a stand near the gate, as his father had done, and he said the crowds were smaller than they used to be but friendlier. Judges walked the livestock barn with clipboards, stopping to look at the teeth of sheep and to ask children how old their goats were. The barn smelled of hay and sawdust, and the floor was covered with straw that stuck to shoes and was tracked out into the sun. The winners were announced over a loudspeaker that crackled whenever the wind changed, and the names were read twice because nobody could hear them the first time. A girl of about ten won a ribbon for a pumpkin so large that two men had to carry it on a board, and her mother cried while the photograph was taken. Down by the river, the tractor pull ran late into the afternoon. Engines roared, tires spun on the dirt, and a cloud of dust drifted over the bleachers. The announcer called out the weight of each pull, and the crowd cheered when a machine cleared a distance no one had managed all day. Families ate corn dogs and funnel cakes from paper trays, and children ran between the rows with prizes won at a ring-toss booth. An older man in a straw hat told anyone who would listen about the year the axle on his tractor broke and how he had walked home in the rain. The fair has always been a place where neighbors who rarely speak during the year stand in line together and talk about weather, prices, and the price of fuel. The high school band played on Saturday, and a local church sold pies by the slice to pay for a new roof. A woman selling jam said the fair was the one week a year when she saw people she had known since school, and she had come every summer since she was a girl. Volunteers kept a lost-child tent near the main gate, and by Saturday evening they had reunited six families, one of them twice. Rain came on Sunday and chased people under the grandstand, where they waited out the storm and watched the mud spread across the track. The storm passed quickly, as summer storms do, and the sun came back just in time to dry the seats before the evening program. When the sky cleared, the last of the rides ran with half-empty seats and the vendors began to pack. Cleanup crews moved through the lanes with carts and brooms, and the bleachers were folded and stacked for another year. By Sunday night the organizers touted record attendance, and the gates were shut on another year of the fair.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context depth test: claimed piece ' touted' (0.47) sits roughly 650 tokens into an ordinary fair narrative containing no other claimed piece, and the context-free, retrospective claim predicts it still fires.
